review:
Cyberpunk as a modern genre has an identity problem. The genre was originally meant to embody what technological advancement could look like if we don't pump the brakes, to show what rampant consumerism and capitalist grind culture could do to our human identity. For all intents and purposes, the "punk" side of cyberpunk was meant to imbue a sense that cyberpunk media is protest art. It's a bleak, but paradoxically beautiful mirror to hold up to our own society; unfortunately, that beauty often undermines its own message.

This is where that aforementioned problem begins. I've recently been consuming a lot of cyberpunk media: the titular Cyberpunk 2077, Neon Giant's The Ascent, and [i]Star Wars Bad Batch[/i], which dabbles in some cyberpunk ideas from time to time. These works transport you to detailed, lived-in, ridiculously beautiful tech wastelands. The lights, the spaceships, the seas of people, and the constant sense of dynamic adventure are all there in many cyberpunk works.

However, that feeling the sci-fi gloss often imparts can contradict with the real problems that the cyberpunk genre seeks to reveal. All the grit doesn't keep you from thinking, "I want to live there, or at least see it." A lot of cyberpunk fiction falls flat as a cautionary tale for this reason.

Booting up Cruelty Squad for the first time took courage. I mean, [i]look[/i] at this thing. The menus, the border around the screen, the massive blob of a health bar, and the brown note soundscape do everything in their power to grate on your senses. Dialogue sounds like something out of an Animal Crossing creepypasta, everyone is obsessed with Chunkopops and Gorbino's Quest, I could go on and on. Cruelty Squad is a deeply, profoundly ugly game; that's a strength, not a weakness.

The world of Cruelty Squad is so far down the corporate hypercapitalist rabbit hole that it doesn't even matter anymore. The rich have figured out how to come back from death itself, so the value of human life has dropped far below 0. Everyone in Cruelty Squad's world is either obsessed with some product lifestyle, corporate fad, or doing enough drugs to be able to keep up with both. The player character is a member of the Cruelty Squad, a privately owned contract killer organization that does the bidding of larger conglomerates obsessed with their bottom line. This game's world is just oozing with venom for the corporate future we could be heading towards, and you can see that in every frame.

Cruelty Squad's transgressive design doesn't keep it from being a damn good immersive sim. Each level tasks you with killing  a target or two and escaping, which is simple enough on paper. In practice, your preferred playstyle could send you on a unique route through the level due to the game's open-ended design. Shoot open doors, break vents in the ceiling, grapple hook through windows, or barge through the front door if you'd like; Cruelty Squad's commitment to player freedom is strong, so strong that you can completely glitch out of the map to beat levels if you want to.

There are heaps upon heaps of secret weapons, augments, and missions to find throughout the world, lending replay value to the game's campaign. Although the AI is ArmA 3 jank tier at all times, the enemies are dangerous and the time to kill is low. The secrets, the open level design, and the dangerous enemies all force you to really look at what you're playing, which is a great way to pull you into Cruelty Squad's twisted world.

Cruelty Squad is rotten. The game imbues its ideas and messages about corporate greed and consumer culture into its world so deftly that you could be mistaken for thinking the mess of textures and assaulting soundscape of its world were thrown together haphazardly; make no mistake, the hideousness, the true grit of Cruelty Squad's world is absolutely intentional. This is a cyberpunk (although some might call it biopunk but that's splitting hairs) work that actually has something to say, and expects you to agree; I don't want to go to Cruelty Squad's world, and the game nods along with my assessment.

In its final hours, Cruelty Squad gets very abstract and existential. A huge portion of the community's discourse around this game involves Cruelty Squad's endings and what they imply about the game world and our own. This is one of those games I'd expect forums to light up about for years to come, debating its true meaning and finding value in the nonsense. Don't ask me to make sense of it because I barely could, but what I got instead was an experience both unique and truly cyberpunk.

Cruelty Squad's critique of our world is laser focused and wrapped in a package brimming with secrets, and that makes me a happy little flesh ape. It's absolutely worth the price tag, and it's worth pushing through the grime to see the message just underneath.

All jokes aside, here is an actual review of the game:

First off, it's really good. Really good game. Super unique and I'm loving it.

Once you get used to the cursed graphics and get a hang of the unconventional controls (this reload mechanic is unique asf, and R is interact?!), youll quickly notice how SMOOTH this game experience is.

It's a Hitman game, where each mission is a new location, with a target(s) that you have to kill, and once you kill them, you locate the exit and Mission Complete! You also can see your target through the walls at ALL times so you know exactly where they are and what direction to go. There are innocent civilians wandering the map as well as a number of armed security guards.

There's CRACKED bhop movement, you can bunny hop like a right tweaker at 60mph across the whole map, and later upgrades will further crack out your already cracked movement.

So... you start a mission, know exactly where your target is, bunny hop like hell to the target, blast them, bunny hop to the exit and beat the entire mission in less than a minute.
...if you want!

The large secret-filled environments mixed with the lack of a time limit means you can move at whatever pace you want, and the only way to unlock new weapons (there are at least a couple dozen) is by finding it on that stage and carrying it with you to the Exit. Once you do this you can now choose to equip that weapon on any mission. This mechanic rewards you for exploring and not going directly to the target every mission, since later levels will be super difficult with only the default silenced pistol and smg. These weapons can be found in a dedicated spot somewhere in the map, or can be picked up from dead enemies. 

You're enticed to replay previous levels as you unlock more stuff, since your new abilities will allow you to access parts of the map that were otherwise unreachable on your first attempt.

It's also pretty funny. Dialogue made me laugh out loud a few times. Every single NPC talks to you when interacted with.

I have no idea how far into the game I am, for sure less than halfway, and am excited to see how crazy it gets later on in the game (I've already unlocked some massive weapons and have seen some insane, building-sized enemies). It's been something that I find myself opening every other day to either play through a new level or return to previous ones.

Oh and there's also a stock market to invest in, obviously. Press Tab at any point during your violent shootouts to FOMO your blood money away :)

I really highly recommend this even at it's $19.99 price-point. There's a TON of content and is worth every penny. You can tell it's developed by a passionate, unique individual who really knows how to make a fun (and fresh) game, and I can't wait to see what they continue to create.

Cruelty Squad is one of the best, if not the best game to come out of 2021. 

I bought this game at a pivotal time in my life, moving out and living on my own. It's hard to describe truly, how excited I was to make my own life and prove myself to the world. Nobody looming over my neck, nobody making decisions for me, freedom. Freedom to do with my time as I saw fit.

Playing it for an hour or two, I thought it was okay. A very wacky immersive sim. Nothing to write home about beyond the unorthodox controls and deliberate assault on the eyes. I looked to other games soon after.

A few weeks later I found myself in a situation where I needed money and I needed a lot. I had to pay for my apartment which I was leasing by myself. I had one friend where I moved, so I was mostly just stuck looking after myself. Stuck in this limbo, constantly jumping that hurdle I never thought I could clear. 

Out of this desperation, I started working at Amazon.

It was truly, one of the most grueling experiences of my life. Just over the entrance to the "Fulfillment Center", a large blue smile looms over you. It's not exactly giving the intended effect, and certainly not the warm welcome you're expecting. 

You're in this building, this big, bland building for 10 hours putting cheap Chinese packages in receptacles. You don't speak with anyone and you get two thirty minute breaks. Occasionally there will be a supervisor coming to either tell you to pick up the pace or to tell you that you're doing well. You're always reminded of your speed. You're always doing well, but never well enough.

What was this all for, anyway? Why was I doing this? If I follow through, and work these grueling hours, I'm just gonna spend my three days off resting and feeling the worry of coming back in a few days just to do it all over again. Again and again until you die. You're put on this earth to work and buy until you die.

I'll never forget the moment where I was working at a station just down the hall from a man with about 3 or 4 teeth. It was one of the few times I was looking at someone and we were just barely within earshot of each other. He told me he did this job to pay for treating his son, who was suffering from brain cancer. He was unkempt, clearly lacking sleep. He teared up just telling me all that he'd went through, before a supervisor politely cut in and asked the both of us to focus on our work.

Why do I bring all of this up? Because on one of my off days, I needed something to clear my mind. Something to help me forget about the Brazil-esque hallways with incomprehensible, almost imposing machinery surrounding me, juxtaposed by unsettling corporate imagery telling me to "chin up". I booted up Cruelty Squad and what I found was a scathing critique of modern work culture.

You play as a hitman working a gig job. Every assignment you take is through an app on your phone. In every level, you are assigned with killing people who have wronged the company that you (and presumably your boss) are working for. Lines like "We'll be free to install a new CEO who is more compatible with the concept of mass scale human sacrifice" come to mind.

There is an organ market in which life is given a constantly shifting price, and anybody can invest. You cannot just buy a house from working your nine-to-five job. You need to take risks and make investments. You need to get implants for your organs so that you can do your job more efficiently. You need to do your job faster and get the perfect ranks to earn even more money. You're always doing your job well, but never well enough.

Nowhere is the messaging of this game more clear than the Office level. It is the best level in this entire game. You begin looking away from the office, staring at a small pond, almost modest in it's nature, but as you pan away from the pond, you bear witness to this monolithic office building, towering over you, the pond, and every surrounding building.

It's maze-like in nature. You're constantly moving up and down between the floors searching for 4 very similar targets before rising up an elevator to the very top floor. A CEO sits behind her desk, and if you decide to talk to her, she says: [b] "Shouldn't you be at work?" [/b]

Even the music for this level is the absolute peak of the soundtrack, perfectly telling you what this game has to say about your life as a worker. It begins with what sounds like a drilling noise, followed by a hammer-ish smashing noise. both come together with even more cruel-sounding noise in the background. Bells ring followed by a choir. It's almost melancholic in tone, giving you this reflective feeling. Why are you doing this? Why are you grinding your life away to please people who would never give you the chance to be in their position?

The beat disappears and the choir comes into full swing, truly amplifying this effect. You've wasted your life. You're in an office building, killing the same person over, and over and over. Why [i] are [/i] you doing this? 

Finally, the drilling, hammering beat comes back. You're just a tool in the same way someone would use a drill or a hammer, an affordable solution for corporate liquidation. Why are you doing this? Because there is no other way. This is your life until you die. 

[b] DIVINE LIGHT SEVERED. YOU ARE A FLESH AUTOMATON ANIMATED BY NEUROTRANSMITTERS. [/b]

Cruelty Squad is definitely one of the most multi-layered and eye melting games I've ever played. Multi-layered in regards to initial perception of course.

Cruelty Squad is essentially a first person assassination game where a monstrous looking corporate overlord sends you on murder missions for dollary doo's and shits and giggles. The game frequently jumps back and forth between actual commentary and a depraved sense of humour. The genius of Cruelty Squad is that it looks like a pure shitpost of a game, but in reality its far smarter than most other games in its genre.

The game is level based, taking place across 13 main missions including the intro. There are also a bunch of secret levels for those brave enough to find them. Typically you'll be tasked with eliminating 1 or more targets for the sake of protecting your corporate overlords.

Despite the game's extremely harsh and crude aesthetic, visually and audibly, there is a clear vision beneath it all. The world of Cruelty Squad is truly filthy, but hiding beneath a false pretence of luxury. Most of the people here live for their mediocrity and in a sense, so do you. Your job is to murder people without question, and of course you do this, because this world has taught you this is the only way to pay your bills.

Money is gained by doing missions and playing the stock market. You can buy and sell traditional stocks, but you can also trade human body parts and fish. Enemies that you kill can have their organs harvested, which then become stocks which you can hold onto or sell. The same goes for fish. By finding a fishing rod in one of the earlier levels, you can go fishing and then play them on the stock market for additional gains. These elements are fun and well designed, but they also play into the world itself. Everything that isn't immediately relevant to your murder missions is used for pure capital. Fish, organs and stocks simply serve to add extra zero's to your bank and everything exists to help you become a more efficient murderer.

Without going into spoilers, the ending genuinely left me speechless for a moment and gave me new insight into the entire experience. The game only took me around 7 hours to beat, but its a wild ride for the whole way through.

It's a must play if you're a fan of fps, no joke.

One of the first things you'll see in Cruelty Squad is a mass shooting. A man, armed with a light machine gun, is mowing down civilians in an open plaza. Blood and bodies pile up. Unsettling chiptune music plays over the scene. Your character watches the mayhem from his apartment window high above. He looks unfazed, content even. He's on the phone, but he's not calling the police. More important things to attend to.

A gig offer. Corporate assassination. You accept.

The reality of Cruelty Squad is an all-consuming nightmare. Distorted textures, unsettling characters, glitchy corrupted soundscapes pummel you at every opportunity. Overwhelming at first, you adapt after an hour or so to the relatively simple Hitman-style objectives. Load in, kill your marks, and get out. Earn cash to buy new equipment, ranging from mundane tools like Kevlar vests and frag grenades, to the disturbing, like a skullgun that damages you every time you fire. Of particular note is the Grappendix, its grotesque appearance matched by its game-breaking utility. Get it as soon as you can. Level secrets and strange gameplay mechanics add tons of replayability to your experience, and the real-time stock market simulation can allow you to sell the organs of the people you kill, and even react to certain events in the game. A savvy investor can make out like a bandit, if you know how to time the market.

The gameplay of Cruelty Squad is good, damn good. If that was all there was to it, CS would be just another good indie title with a unique aesthetic. And while that's perfectly fine, to leave it there would be missing the treasure behind the trash.

The infinite desire for ever greater power, progress, and profit has corrupted the world and its inhabitants. Day to day life revolves around work, consuming products, and transaction-based creation myths. Owning property is a heavenly utopia. Adopting a CEO mindset and burying your friends under the unstoppable might of capital with a grin on your face is viewed with godly admiration. Life has no value besides the organs under your skin. Remember at the start of the game those people getting mowed down in the streets? Watch the cutscene again and pay attention to the bystanders. See how they aren't making any attempt to get out of the way? They look bored. Just as bored as the protagonist watching from above. They all realize how meaningless their lives are. Your targets will even talk with you, their soon-to-be killer, if you're so inclined. Some will insult you, others indifferent. Yet others happy even, to have someone listen about their troubles. Self-preservation is an odd trait to have in Cruelty Squad. Who cares about dying when coming back is so easy?

On a more literal note, I believe this title was made by an artist deeply disgusted by our capitalistic fetishization of wealth and the figureheads that embody those productive virtues (Elon, Bezos, Thiel, Stark, etc...). Cruelty Squad's universe revels in the trauma loop one can find themselves trapped in when their finances hang by teetering balances, at risk of disruption by powers outside of their control. When your health insurance doesn't cover a devastating surprise medical bill, Cruelty Squad sneers and grins and tells you to keep up that grindset. When a loan is denied because of a credit score, Cruelty Squad shrugs with contempt and suggests lining the walls of your room with Funko Pops. It even has something to say about the GameStop short squeeze. Try putting your savings into the "GamesGames" stock. You won't be disappointed.

I love Cruelty Squad. I also hate it, but I think Cruelty Squad does as well. To spare you with specifics, I found my sentiment with the game to roughly follow the vibe of each of the game's major narrative beats. Over time I saw the deep-fried aesthetic not with nausea, but hatred. An intense hatred to the all-consuming cancer that capitalism has gripped this world in. The game shares in all this anger, all this rage. It's punk. It's classic punk. It's punk in the way only a murder simulator could scream its message at the cancer to go fuck itself. It's one of the deepest connections I've ever felt with a game. It's art. It's garbage. It's the last game I would have ever expected to leave such an impact on my life. Grab your favorite gun, load up a level, and get liquidating. You've got stocks to buy.

There's a particular existential angst I feel, reflected in this game. Like grocery shopping at a walmart after helping your cancer-ridden mother navigate insurance bureaucracy. Like sitting on the soggy, stained, 40+ year old carpet of a run down singlewide you just dropped 500K on, and contemplating that this dreary moment is blinding levels of success. Its capitalist enshittification, incarnate, distilled into a game. Everything sucks by design, working as intended.
There's a moment I like: "Only good things will come to one like you".
The rotten smile of late stage capitalism, speaking to its billionaires, its chosen champions.

Its a wonderfully crafted piece of punk art, and hits especially close to home with the state of the world these days.

I'm not very skilled at shooters, and played it for the "story"; but gameplay wise, its a rock throwing duel between windows. The AI is barebones, but melts you instantly if you allow them to see you for more than a second. You're meant to bunnyhop about at breakneck speeds, deleting targets in the blink of an eye, and its very polished in that aspect.
Another aspect I came to feel, is that you're guided to win through "dirty tricks", jank, quick and lazy solutions. The office level comes to mind - you could fight your way up the floors, a long and grueling battle where failing to headshot one guard in time will send you back to the start. Or you could just shoot out the windows, and watch the targets eagerly jump out. Done in seconds, without even stepping foot in the building.
There's idiot party, a similar, entire elaborate tower to descend and fight through. Or you can just drop down the elevator shaft and you're done. There's always some incredibly efficient solution, hidden in plain sight. There's probably an intentional metaphor in that.

As others have said, an incredible amount of thought and effort went into this. Its a great game, very polished, and truly something to be experienced by anyone who can stomach it.

Cruelty Squad looks like utter jank at first glance. And even on subsequent close inspections. Every texture is atrocious. It breaks every rule of UI design, nothing is intuitive, and it looks like placeholder art from start to finish.

Then you realize: it's the Sweet Bro and Hella Jeff approach. It's so deliberately and consistiently awful, it requires actual effort, a commitment to aesthetic that flips right back around to downright impressive.

And that aesthetic is quite possibly what the world would look like to someone who's absolutely batshit insane, so detached from everything that they make the guy from Hatred look like a perfectly normal guy by comparison. I mean, it was in the description, you're a depressed gunman and detached from everything, but it's hard to understand just how detached that can be.

And under it all, some relatively robust gunplay, a weird-but-interesting reload mechanic, and horripilatingly cyberpunk descriptions and setting.

It's an experience. Price point's on the uncomfortable side, but worthwhile.
YT comment says it the best: "The developer put thousands of hours into crafting one of the most cohesive and tight indie FPS games in years, then spent twice as long making it seem like he didn't."

Probably one of the most unique games I've ever played. On the surface it looks like something a 12 year old would make, it's ugly, off-putting, uncomfortable, and sometimes incomprehensible but there's actually a really good game hidden beneath the layer of aesthetic gunk. 

The devs of this game really went out of their way to make this game look like it had zero effort put into it, but it's secretly a very polished and addicting immersive sim, you take on the role of a grunt of the Cruelty Squad, a subsidiary company that tasks you with finding and eliminating suits of rival companies to better their own.
 To tell you the truth I didn't understand most of this game's story but I do like how this game depicts augmentations/body enhancements of the future, for example all the modifications you get for your body are really gross and not very cool at all, like a dash ability creates holes in your back that you shoot waste out of, and another one takes out half of your skull in a really grotesque way to implant a skull gun in your brain to shoot enemies with. This game has a really bleak depiction of the future, everything in this game is suffering there's death everywhere and it's completely normalized because society is so used to things being awful in the future and I find it really interesting compared to other cyberpunk games.

If I had to describe the gameplay it feels sort of like Deus Ex mixed with Hitman, in each level you have a number of targets you have to eliminate and there's a large variety of ways to take them out similar to Hitman,but it has a very similar level structure and gameplay style to Deus Ex, it does feel much faster paced and more arcadey than both of those games though. 
You start with a maximum of two weapons and can begin with a number of body augmentations, each one completely changing your playstyle and you can find and unlock more to add to your starting roster by finding them inside levels, you can also find new weapons and take them back with you to start with in the level select, all you have to do is reach the exit holding it and it's yours. 
This game also has TONS of secrets all over the place, alternate routes to make completing levels easier, hidden weapons and upgrades, weird easter eggs and strange things to experience, and my personal favorite secret levels. You can find entirely new levels through secret exits in the base levels of this game and most of them are pretty hard but lots of fun and they also have secrets inside of them that are worth looking for.
 I think if you're playing this game and not looking for secrets you're missing half of the fun of it in my opinion because that's where I got most of my enjoyment from, replaying levels and searching it up and down for secrets and trying out different loadouts to see what works the best was really fun and never got old.

There's so so soooo much more I can talk about with this game, every aspect of this game is so dense and detailed but I think if any of this sounds interesting to you, you should check it out for yourself and discover everything on your own if you can stomach the presentation that is because underneath you'll find a very unique and addicting immersive sim/tactical shooter.

Cruelty Squad is one of a kind. It's a challenging tactical shooter: You choose your starting weapons and mission equipment, hunt down 2 or 3 targets in an open level, and exfiltrate. It's somewhat reminiscent of the old Rainbow Six games, except that you don't get to control a squad and that there are light imsim elements allowing you to explore different routes, crawl into vents, carry around trash cans, throw exploding toxic toilets, and talk to civilians. A bit like Thief, with similarly confusing levels. Enemies aim sharp and if you die, you restart the mission from scratch. The only thing that stands out at the beginning is a stock market simulation that allows you to generate passive income from your mission rewards, which you can use later to buy better armor or other upgrades to lower the sometimes crushing difficulty. Oh, and there are needlessly complex fishing and organ harvesting mechanics, too. But none of these mechanics particularly stand out in comparison with other games in the genre, so rather than the gameplay, you are mostly drawn back by the weirdness: graphics that look like they were drawn in MS Paint, a soundtrack that sounds like it was composed in MS Paint, and NPCs talking to you as if written by someone who spends way too much time in MS Paint. You can play the game like this, finish all the main missions, watch the ending, and move on to a different game after 5 hours.

...or you can put 10 more hours in and dive below its surface. Once you get closer to the end, pile up money, and buy some body implants, you might realize that Cruelty Squad is filled to the brim with secret unlockables that are almost impossible to find without a guide: levels, weapons, implants, even difficulty modes that open previously locked doors and spawn unique enemies. Your new upgrades will gradually break the game, you will transcend the tactical shooter gameplay and become one with the audiovisual drug hellscape. You will think less about sniping heads from cover and instead grapple and glitch through nooks and crannies that had before eluded your thoughts. Together with the bizarre elaborate lore that is filled with references to the most obscure shit and has been pieced together by players (partially through data mining), even after you beat all the missions, saw all the endings, and unlocked all the equipment, Cruelty Squad will never give you the feeling that you are even close to having seen everything that it has to offer.

However, none of this means that the game is terribly meaningful or based on a masterful plan. From what it feels like and from what the dev shared on Twitter, Cruelty Squad is really just his Godot learning project where he threw in one weird mechanic after another that was later discovered and deciphered by players entirely by chance. The game goes against many established design principles and probably would not have survived, had it not drawn in a commited community with its absurd art direction. And most of all, it is a testament to how creativity and innovation can completely overshadow graphic fidelity, technical standards, handholding, and pretty much everything else that most games stand for by taking the safe route even if built on but not expanding on an interesting foundation. It's just like Gorbino's Quest.

Where do I even begin to talk about Cruelty Squad? This game is so exceptionally bizarre, surreal and unique and has so much going on with it that I can’t help but begin with the most immediate surface level details: the aesthetics, and then try and work deeper from there. Keep in mind whilst reading this review, Cruelty Squad sets out to make a bizarre and alien feeling world by subverting 30 odd years of conventional game design wisdom. It aspires to recapture a childlike feeling of games appearing limitless – like you could find almost anything within them, and it strives to achieve this feeling by deviating completely from tradition in terms of aesthetics, mechanics and narrative.

So first off: the aesthetics. Cruelty Squad’s art-style is surrealist and unconventional, everything they would teach you in art school is deliberately reversed: text will zoom in too large, colours are always conflicting opposites, the use of screen-space is thrown out the window with the metallic/fleshy border surrounding your screen. And its not just the art that is an assault on the senses, the music, likewise, is full of slurping noises and tortured synths. All of this supports the game’s goal of subverting norms and creating an alien feeling world.

The mechanics, similarly, goes completely against every other FPS I’ve ever played: R is interact, F is kick, and to reload you have to right-click and then pull your mouse down and then up. The surface level of aesthetics and mechanics can be quite hostile towards the player in how uncomfortable and unfamiliar it is. Cruelty Squad’s game design is much more familiar, however, wearing its influences from titles such as Deus Ex and Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six on its sleeve. Each mission you drop into a level with only one goal: assassinate your targets. Following the design of immersive sims, the level is one open playground for you to explore and find multiple varying routes to achieve your goal. Coming from Deus Ex, I felt right at home sneaking through vents and sniping enemies with a silenced pistol. And that isn’t where the similarities end, you can also find as well as purchase body augmentations that give you abilities such as: a double jump, grapple hook, speed boost, enemy sensor and much more to find creative solutions to assassinating targets. The arsenal of weapons at your disposal is large, ranging from conventional weaponry to DNA scramblers and rifles that do damage based on your stock holdings. The time to kill and be killed is very low in this game, but both tactical stealth as well as daring high speed run and gun tactics (with augments) are viable gameplay options. Having touched on the familiar, Cruelty Squad is also the only FPS I know of to have a fully functional stock market, organ harvesting black market, and fishing minigame (and fish market) all in one.

So whats the justification for all this rampant murder in universe? Your character is a mercenary who used to work for the government run “SEC Death Unit” before being recruited by the “Cruelty Squad” – a company tasked with the “liquidations” of the enemies of its parent conglomerate. In this dystopian corporatocracy, corporations not only have complete control over the entire world, but advances in technology allows for the resurrection of the dead, rendering human life not just worthless, but of negative value. The game’s narrative feels like an eclectic mix of ideas and themes the creator was contemplating at the time of development. The game doesn’t try and force the ideas it presents, and like all good art its up to the individual to filter the text through their own experiences. In my own interpretation, the main ideas Cruelty Squads presents is that of a corporatocratic/late stage capitalist dystopia, Gnosticism, and the philosophy of Bataille. The creation myth for the world of Cruelty Squad is that of the creation of a free market – and here we see that capitalism in the game is steeped in mythology. CEO’s are almost godlike, corporations are all powerful and all pervasive, and it is the technology spawned of this system that conquers death. Furthermore, we see a Gnostic worldview/filter applied to this corporatocratic system. In simple terms, Gnosticism puts forth the belief that the world was created by an evil being and that the material world is a wretched prison that separates people from the light of god. The multiple endings of the game each give a different reaction / course of action in response to this oppressive society / earthly prison where human life has become “worthless” and cut off from the divine light of god.

In conclusion, the gameplay of assassinating targets in large and complex levels with an entire arsenal of different tools and abilities to vary your approach is fun. The style of the game is unique, and creates the feeling of an interesting and alien game world where you don’t know what to expect will come next. I also found myself contemplating the games themes and symbolism well after finishing the game and enjoyed researching various topics to flesh out my understanding. Not to mention, all the absurd stories that come out of this game that you’ve most likely already seen in other steam reviews. I recommend Cruelty Squad to people who are familiar with the timeline of classic fps games and are interested in a game that subverts the 30 odd years of game design convention we’ve come to expect in interesting ways. I also recommend this game to anyone just looking to try a unique gaming experience, to explore a bizarre virtual world, and I think you will know if this is you just by taking a look at the screenshots of the game. Cruelty Squad is a difficult game to talk about, and I certainly don’t do it justice in this review, but if anything in this review or just the screenshots on steam catch your interest, give this game a shot – its an incredible game to get lost in.

Cruelty Squad is a game in the style of Hitman or Deus Ex, where you're tasked to kill targets on levels that have multiple paths and approaches.

But first, it has to be said: this is the best example of a postmodernist game. It ignores (and mocks) staples of game designs such as "having good/pleasant graphics", "good enemy and NPC" AI, "have an intuitive UI" or "have a professional, consistent soundtrack", yet it all makes perfect sense given the style of the game, and the universe it's set on, and it creates something that is better than the sum of it's parts. 

It's a labor of love, a game that transcends what you expect from game studios, and instead focuses on the things that truly matter to a dedicated player: a great sense of discovery thanks to the wacky game design choices, the different approaches you get your objectives, and tons of unlockables that DO matter and affect the way you play. Also, secrets, lots of secrets, from lore related dialogue, to weapons and equipment, bonus levels and difficulties/game modes.

There's a lot to unpack about this game, but I think it's better that you play the game yourself, and slowly discover all the things it has to offer.

The only warning I can give is that the game is hard. Really hard. There's no mid-level saves, and the beginning is tough, because you have no special weapons or augments, and you must rely on stealth, precise aim and learning the way the AI behaves. But once you get past that, there's a lot of fun to be had, trust me.

Also the game is gory and violent, so you must be prepared for that.

INDUSTRIAL SOCIETY AND ITS FUTURE
Introduction

1. The Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for the human race. They have greatly increased the life-expectancy of those of us who live in “advanced” countries, but they have destabilized society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to indignities, have led to widespread psychological suffering (in the Third World to physical suffering as well) and have inflicted severe damage on the natural world. The continued development of technology will worsen the situation. It will certainly subject human beings to greater indignities and inflict greater damage on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater social disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased physical suffering even in “advanced” countries.

2. The industrial-technological system may survive or it may break down. If it survives, it MAY eventually achieve a low level of physical and psychological suffering, but only after passing through a long and very painful period of adjustment and only at the cost of permanently reducing human beings and many other living organisms to engineered products and mere cogs in the social machine. Furthermore, if the system survives, the consequences will be inevitable: There is no way of reforming or modifying the system so as to prevent it from depriving people of dignity and autonomy.

3. If the system breaks down the consequences will still be very painful. But the bigger the system grows the more disastrous the results of its breakdown will be, so if it is to break down it had best break down sooner rather than later.

4. We therefore advocate a revolution against the industrial system. This revolution may or may not make use of violence; it may be sudden or it may be a relatively gradual process spanning a few decades. We can’t predict any of that. But we do outline in a very general way the measures that those who hate the industrial system should take in order to prepare the way for a revolution against that form of society. This is not to be a POLITICAL revolution. Its object will be to overthrow not governments but the economic and technological basis of the present society.

5. In this article we give attention to only some of the negative developments that have grown out of the industrial-technological system. Other such developments we mention only briefly or ignore altogether. This does not mean that we regard these other developments as unimportant. For practical reasons we have to confine our discussion to areas that have received insufficient public attention or in which we have something new to say. For example, since there are well-developed environmental and wilderness movements, we have written very little about environmental degradation or the destruction of wild nature, even though we consider these to be highly important.

Cruelty Squad is a disgusting game. It sounds, and feels EXACTLY how it looks.

From this point onward, everything that I'm gonna be saying is coming from a mind filled with praise.

Yes, I am PRAISING this abomination.

Right from the get go, right within the first 10 seconds, you feel completely and utterly repulsed by the art direction. Deliberately abrasive and uncanny. Like visual sandpaper. One of the clearest examples of anti aesthetic design in modern games. Sickly neon colors, hostile UI design, fleshy coloring, strange biotech motifs. It weaponizes ugliness, sensory overload, and retro tech surrealism to produce a world that feels extremely heavy, corrupted, and spiritually rotten to the core. There's not a single redeemable thing about it and this reflects the game's atmosphere perfectly. The aesthetic that Cruelty Squad goes for is essentially a cross between Cyberpunk 2077, LSD: Dream Simulator, the most disgusting metropolis sewage system you could ever imagine, and the mental state of a heavily drunk Finnish man who has already gone through 4 rounds of Russian Roulette. There are some people who would call Cruelty Squad's art direction as "Vomitpunk", and that is legitimately a perfectly apt description of it. There is no beauty in this game. None. And that is what makes it beautiful.

To sum up the soundtrack? 

It feels like what could play in your head during the groggy recovery phase after a highly intensive and dangerous surgery. Ringing in your skull, the taste of blood coating your mouth, drugs surging through your veins as you try your best not to cry too hard and accidentally pull out the IV. It sounds like what would play when you are succumbing to a disgustingly corporate lifestyle. Devoid of humanity, used as a tool. Working a completely soul sucking job and praying for release that never comes.
At its best, the music sounds as depressing than Pokemon's Lavender Town theme. 
At its worst, it sounds like what would play in someone's mind while they are having a seizure. 
And sometimes, it sounds like an upset stomach, churning up whatever you ate for breakfast for the nuclear projectile vomit that will occur moments later.
Neat stuff.

I mean, the game opens up with the protagonist, an unnamed cybernetically and biotechnologically altered mercenary, taking a shower after being fired from his job as an SEC Death Squad unit and then staring out of his apartment building, observing a poor soul flip the hell out and causing a mass shooting. 
This protagonist, who is known as MT Foxtrot (lovingly referred to as Empty F*ck) by the playerbase, does nothing to stop this, as he recieves a phonecall from a corporate entity that treats him less than human, offering him a job as a mercenary. 
He says nothing over the phone. 
He accepts the job offer.
He is a disposable corporate asset, only used to carry out the will of his greedy overlords.

Really sets the tone, doesn't it?

The moment you take control of this protagonist, if you can even call it “control” when your body feels like a wet prosthetic limb, you understand fully that Cruelty Squad does not want you to succeed. Or feel competent. Or remotely comfortable. The game’s moment to moment mechanics are a direct extension of its vomit slicked aesthetic, that being uniquely clumsy, hostile, gelatinous, and spiritually bankrupt.

Movement feels like you are piloting a reanimated corpse with a GPU from 1997 bolted to its spine.
Guns kick like industrial machinery that resent the fact you touched them.
Getting hit is less “damage taken” and more “a reminder of your pathetic meat existence.”
The simple act of reloading your firearms isn't just pressing the R button like in other FPS games, you actually have to freeze in place, hold down the right mouse button, and flick the camera downwards. Speaking of firearms, instead of ADSing with right click, you have to use the shift button. Ergonomically atrocious. It feels tactical in the best worst way possible.

Overall, Cruelty Squad’s gameplay loop is the purest distillation of gig economy violence:
You clock in, execute some corporate rivals, harvest a few organs, and pray your stock portfolio doesn’t crater because you bought the wrong type of spleen futures. Yes, you can invest in the stockmarket in this game. Try to get enough money to afford that freaking intestine umbilical cord grappling hook, and no, that is NOT hyberbole. It exists in the game. I kid you not, you can swing from building to building with a fleshy tendril growing out of your stomach like spider man. And here's more disgusting things to strap to your body in order to gain an advantage in combat. 

Imagine stapling malfunctioning fleshy medical equipment directly to your organs because your boss told you it might “improve productivity.” Faster legs that jerk your body like a cockroach on a hot stove. Eyes that turn the world into an irradiated funhouse of God’s regret. Yes. Have fun with that.

Every mechanic is designed to make you feel like a malfunctioning biotech marionette tripping through a series of corporate mandated murders. It feels relentlessly janky as hell. A strange and unconventional mix of the original Deus Ex and Hitman in terms of gameplay feel. 

And, with all of this context in mind, it is perfect.

In order to recommend Cruelty Squad, the first thing we need to do is describe what it IS and what it ISN'T. Cruelty Squad isn't exactly an Immersive Sim, nor is it a pulse-pounding Arcade Shoot-Em-Up or 'Neo-Boomer Shooter' to use the parlance of our times. If I had to compare this game to anything, I'd liken it to what happens when Rainbow Six, Hotline Miami, and SWAT 4 get put into a microwave together. In short, Cruelty Squad is a psychedelic tactical romp through a bizarre biopunk world where not even death is absolute.

Donning the neon-green shades of the player (affectionately-referred to by fans as 'EMPTY FUCK'), you are employed by the titular 'Cruelty Squad'--a private assassination firm with the express purpose of delivering cruelty and pain to whomever their contractor points at. Your missions pit you against manic corporate execs, mutant police, deranged cult leaders, and even a demonic CEO or two. For any other game this would be wacky, but for Cruelty Squad it's just the daily grind. Moreso in that thanks to breakthroughs in genetics and biology, no one in Cruelty Squad can ever truly DIE as long as their DNA is intact enough to be cloned, you included.

Needless to say, Cruelty Squad's world is a nihilistic playground full of maniacs and freaks looking for the newest fix to cope with the crippling realization that death just doesn't HAPPEN anymore. While this sounds somewhat depressing on paper, it allows you the player to assassinate people over and over again for a quick buck while using said bucks to invest in the in-game stock market and bioaugmentations! Not a stocks man? Why not sell the organs of your hapless victims or fish you catch during a mission? You don't even get a slap on the wrist for civilian casualties, so why not, right? As mentioned above, your money allows you to invest in a newer, better you with a wide array of goodies: swing across the map like a freakish Spider-Man using the GRAPPENDIX! Get the drop on your foes with the foul-smelling STEALTH SUIT! Running low on gun juice? Install an AMMO GLAND and have your body produce all-natural GMO-free ammunition for your weapons! The only limit is your creativity!

Using the aforementioned goodies, the game drops you into a Deus Ex-sized map and gives you a few targets to ice. As mentioned before, Cruelty Squad is more tactical than it lets on--the player's more fragile than you think and healing items are scarce, so nine times out of ten your success will hinge on your ability to get the drop on your enemies. Don't be scared off, though--you keep any weapons you pick up in a level and collecting new augments usually leads to unlocking new paths for easier takedowns. Even death can have its benefits: die too many times and you'll gain a whole new batch of useful abilities!

Graphics and audio aren't usually pertinent when I review a game, but I feel obligated to talk about them for this one. Cruelty Squad may look strange at best, nauseating at worst, but once you get a feel for the user interface you might grow to enjoy it! As for the sounds, you'll either love it or hate it. Check the game trailers if you want an idea for what you'll be listening to--if you dig it, great! If you don't, there's always a mute option!

I honestly don't have many gripes about Cruelty Squad, but I'd be remiss if I didn't mention them somewhere. My biggest concern with CruSq is that after attempting certain levels a few times (read: the last few), I noticed that while there were enemies placed in static locations, sometimes I'd run into a random enemy completely out of the blue. Certain difficulty levels add/remove enemies to the level, but these ones just seemed to be appearing out of nowhere. Cruelty Squad is a game you pretty much have to accept you're going to bounce off of, maybe a few times. However, as mean and unfair as it is to you with it's difficulty, it gives you many opportunities to break it in retaliation with insane guns and equipment as rewards for exploring and surviving. The gunplay is tight, movement is *incredibly* fast with bunny-hops, double jumps, jet boosters, etc, and there is zero hand-holding.

I think a lot of the frustration can come from how quickly the game tries to alienate you (which is part of the aesthetic, story and world-building) but once you accept you can be as rough to the game as it is with you, it's probably one of the best shooters I've ever played.

if you grew up in the 90s, you've probably been here before. not physically, but this place exists inside your heart. the superheated nightmare of the VHS era, the ugly quaintness of windows 98, the sanitized horror of stomach stapling. maybe you've been here in a nightmare, or maybe the place just sits dormant inside you, like a tumor waiting to be diagnosed. 

cruelty squad is comforting in the same way as that diagnosis; even though it's bad news, there's kind of a peace in knowing for sure. 

the game itself is very fun. it's kind of a combination of deus ex, hitman, and syndicate. you explore strange levels and assassinate strange targets. it's quite challenging, the enemies are reasonable shots and do a lot of damage, but it's fair. there's an emphasis on stealth, but it's not a mission fail if you're detected, it just becomes more challenging. you can outshoot one enemy, but many will be a problem for you.

the variety comes from the large roster of weapons and implants you can pick from, which enable different approaches. pretty much everything is viable, and even goofy seeming weapons have their uses. you can wade in wearing your nightmarish battlesuit and flamethrower everyone on the level, or you can use your intestines to grapple to the top of the tower, kick the target to death, then die to a three foot drop because you replaced all your bones with breadsticks so you could move faster.  I like the pistol that damages your target's DNA so much they explode into an abstract sculpture of viscera, which you can then use to platform on. 

the visual style of the game is painstakingly crafted to be as ugly and strange as possible. the majority of the textures are hand drawn, the rest being made up of heavily processed photos. it means the game looks something like a deep-fried meme. despite that, it's not muddy or confusing, everything is still very readable as enemy or friendly, except for in a handful of areas that are intended to be confusing. 

the music ranges between 'having a fever dream on the couch while the SNES is still on' and 'dead muppets sing in a choir', which helps the surreal atmosphere hugely. the only time it became intrusive was on the first level, where part of the backing track sounded a lot like gunfire which was a bit confusing. 

the level design is both very fun to play and strangely upsetting and scary, like if you ever clipped outside the level in a normal shooter as a child and got freaked out because you found a bunch of blurry, empty rooms and felt trapped and lost. realistic environments blend seamlessly into strangeness, leaving you with a feeling like at any second reality is going to lift away like a peeled off scab. there are many secrets, from alternate routes of attack, to hidden weapons, to full on hidden levels. they are fun to find, but easy to miss, which adds replay value to the levels. 

in general there are a great many secrets and strange game mechanics which are generally not signposted for you, it's a case of discovery. none of it is vital for just completing the game, so you aren't frustrated trying to figure something out so you can progress, it is all hidden side stuff. 

for fans of gorbino's quest there are also a lot of links to the gorbino canon in this game, so don't be surprised if you find a lot of stuff about this game on the various gorbino fan wikis and theory boards. make sure you talk to all the npcs you can to pick up all the nuggets of gorbino lore. there could even be hints about gorbino's quest 2 in here, i've only just started to dive in.

Having truly sucked everything out of the game that I can (save the final final thing), I can comfortably say this is a good one. If you are into carefully considered tactical shooters, this is one of those. I know it doesn't look it, but trust me. It is good, and also, it looks like that on purpose.

Cruelty Squad exists in the same space as the original Dark Souls, where it doesn't care if you don't understand, and will laugh at your lack of understanding. Also like Dark Souls, this game is deep and very considered in terms of its mechanics, and the story, if you happen to care about it. So be in that headspace: it is a deeply ugly S.o.B. that hates you, and doesn't want to be enjoyed. But make no mistake, the gameplay is very tight, easy to control and move, and can get very silly once you start using some of the bodymods.

Presentation: 
The screenshots tell you what you need to know. It is poopoo dogwater tier graphics akin to LSD simulator. Part of the charm. The soundtrack is similarly heinous, but is, again, part of the charm. It is a carefully considered assault of the senses, so if that doesn't sound like something you can handle, don't try. I'm warning you.

Gameplay: 
Careful (or not) tactical shooting. Enemies gib, headshots are almost always an immediate kill, and enemy types that call for different approaches, such as armor-breaking or an enemy lacking a head. You consider your loadout of guns and body-mods and you go off on your adventure. Levels are get in, kill the target(s), and get out, bringing any neat items you've found with you. Think of them as sandboxes to explore and discover secrets within. 

The Story:
It's bananas, man. I won't get into it, but like the Souls games, the story is there if you care, and completely optional if you don't. I will warn you: this is one of those games with a "bitch baby learned nothing" ending, where you get to the end without exploring for secrets. Don't take it personally. My recommendation is, play the game until you reach an ending completely blind, then go in after with outside information. There're some wild things people have done in this game, but you should discover it for yourself, if you can. 

Overview: 
An assault on the senses that hates you and wants you to turn it off. God, why did you buy this? I'll tell you why. The guns feel good and popping heads feels electric. Just try not to think about what it is you're doing, or you may discover there's a reason this world is a complete hellscape.

I got pulled into this game because of all the rave reviews it had been getting. I don't think those reviews are wrong, but I feel like they're aimed at a type of gamer who isn't me, because I didn't enjoy the 5 hours I played of Cruelty Squad.

This is a game where the most interesting mechanics are gated behind grinding for money on tedious fishing and stock market minigames, where levels could be made a third of the size and lose none of their interesting elements, and where extensive parts of the game are spent roaming around mostly empty maps looking for targets or combing for secrets while banal music loops endlessly. Its critiques of the drudgery and soul-sucking nature of modern life are not made more salient by making significant portions of the game itself boring--it merely wastes my time. 

To dwell on that critique of society for a moment--I don't mind when media is deliberately ugly and unpleasant to make a point. Two games I really like are Kane and Lynch 2 and Pathologic 2, games that are often unpleasant to look at, to play, or both. One of my favorite songs is a remix of a washing machine. But this game's aesthetic and tone is like a late Kanye album -- brimming with confidence about its own artistic output that is only sometimes earned. Having your own employer try to kill you because of an accounting error is funny and incisive. Having a slot machine brand called "Jack Off Jack Pot" is GTA-level satire that undermines its own atmosphere. And the game constantly vacillates between a nihilistic critique of the emptiness of modern capitalism and having a double jump powered by yourself pooping, complete with farting sound effect. 

This game wouldn't be half as memorable without its aesthetic, and I don't think that's a bad thing, because the aesthetic is unique and interesting and I'd love to see imitators who refine it. But sometimes I wondered if the game was trying to make me forget about its flaws by attempting to provoke me, or even by implying that the flaws are part of the point. Most of the more obvious ways the game goes against the grain is by making a deliberately ugly interface and mapping some of the player actions to bizarre key combinations, the former of which you get used to quickly, and the latter is easily remedied just by remapping the keys. But it's parts like long stretches of empty space or having a game whose framerate drops despite being absolutely not a graphics- or CPU-intensive game that don't look like intentional flaws--or if they are, they're impossible to distinguish from simply amateur game design. 

The myriad of rave reviews this game has got is testament that a lot of people can really enjoy this game, and you reading this might be one of them. And this game is short and cheap enough that you're not going to have a big loss if you try it out, even if it's not for you. But if you play this game and you end up feeling bored and put off by it and feeling weird by your own lukewarm take on the game in the face of so many positive reviews: rest assured, you are not alone.
